---
title: "Discussion"
---
[] {#sec-discussion}

In this systematic review and Bayesian network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials, vitamin D showed the most consistent evidence of benefit for depressive symptoms among the micronutrients evaluated, particularly in analyses restricted to studies at low-risk-of-bias. By contrast, evidence for anxiety outcomes was inconclusive, and evidence for selenium and other micronutrients was limited by sparse data, imprecision, and substantial heterogeneity. The main implication of these findings is not that micronutrient supplementation is broadly effective for depression and anxiety, but that the current literature is more consistent with a selective and biologically informed interpretation of benefit.

Across low risk-of-bias studies, vitamin D was associated with a modest reduction in depressive symptom severity relative to placebo. That signal is clinically interesting given the broad availability of vitamin D, its generally favorable safety profile when used appropriately, and its biologic relevance to pathways implicated in mood disorders [@sarris_nutritional_2015; @zielinska_dietary_2023; @tobin_targeting_2024]. Vitamin D functions as a neuroactive steroid and has been linked to immune modulation, oxidative stress, neurotrophic signaling, and monoaminergic mechanisms relevant to affective symptoms [@bourre_effects_2006; @wang_zinc_2018; @quan_appropriate_2023]. At the same time, the observed effect should be interpreted with restraint. Between-study heterogeneity was substantial, and the apparent benefit was not uniformly seen across study populations, arguing against a simple conclusion that vitamin D supplementation is effective across all adults with depressive symptoms. The observation that estimated effects were largest in shorter-duration studies (≤8 weeks) and attenuated over longer follow-up may reflect rapid repletion effects that plateau once deficiency is corrected, regression to the mean, or spontaneous remission over time, though the available data do not allow these explanations to be distinguished.

The findings for selenium require even greater caution. Although selenium was associated with a credible reduction in depressive symptoms in the primary analysis, that estimate was derived from a small number of studies with limited sample sizes. Sparse networks can yield unstable estimates, particularly when apparent effects are large. Selenium remains biologically plausible because of its role in antioxidant defense, thyroid hormone metabolism, and inflammatory and neuroendocrine pathways that may intersect with depressive symptoms [@wang_zinc_2018; @majewska_mineral_2025]. However, the current clinical evidence is best viewed as preliminary and hypothesis-generating rather than practice-informing.

For the remaining micronutrients, the absence of statistically credible benefit in low risk-of-bias analyses should not be interpreted as definitive evidence of no effect. For several interventions, including B vitamins, magnesium, zinc, vitamin C, and iron, the available estimates were imprecise, and the credible intervals were wide. This likely reflects a combination of sparse evidence, heterogeneity in dose and formulation, differences in baseline nutrient status and symptom severity, variation in trial duration, and inconsistent outcome measurement [@young_systematic_2019; @zielinska_dietary_2023; @tobin_targeting_2024]. In nutritional psychiatry, pooled null findings may therefore obscure meaningful effects in narrower biologic or clinical subgroups, just as positive findings may be diluted when deficient and replete participants are analyzed together.

 A key contribution of this review is to emphasize baseline micronutrient status, particularly deficiency in relation to depression and anxiety outcomes. Fewer than half of low-risk-of-bias studies (24 of 50; 48%) included participants with deficient pre-intervention levels, defined using established micronutrient-specific thresholds (e.g., vitamin D <20 ng/mL, selenium <70 µg/L, vitamin B6 <20 nmol/L, vitamin B1 <70 nmol/L). Although 24 studies enrolled deficient populations, only sixteen examined the full pathway linking baseline deficiency, supplementation, and depression outcomes. This limits clinical interpretability. Trials that enroll heterogeneous populations containing both deficient and replete individuals may underestimate the effect of repletion by averaging across participants with materially different biologic starting points [@young_systematic_2019; @tobin_targeting_2024]. The present findings are therefore more consistent with a deficiency-informed framework than with a universal supplementation model. In that framework, micronutrients are not understood as nonspecific treatments for all depressive or anxiety symptoms, but as potentially relevant interventions in subgroups with biologically meaningful deficiency.

This interpretation was most clearly supported for vitamin D. Secondary analyses suggested that baseline deficiency and baseline depression status were associated with larger estimated effects of vitamin D, but these findings should be interpreted cautiously because they reflect study-level rather than patient-level effect modification and are therefore more vulnerable to bias and overinterpretation [@zielinska_dietary_2023; @tobin_targeting_2024; @schandelmaier_development_2020]. Vitamin D was also the only nutrient for which the evidence base was sufficiently developed to support this degree of subgroup exploration, which limits broader conclusions about other micronutrients. Even so, these results strengthen the rationale for future trials that stratify or enrich enrollment according to baseline nutrient status rather than assuming homogeneous treatment effects across clinically diverse populations.

The clinical implications of these findings are accordingly narrower than broad enthusiasm for “supplements” might suggest. The present evidence does not support indiscriminate micronutrient supplementation for depression or anxiety. Rather, it supports a cautious and evidence-based approach in which targeted assessment and correction of deficiency may have a role in selected patients. Although micronutrients are often perceived as inherently benign, that assumption should not substitute for clinical judgment. Dose-related toxicity, variable efficacy, and potential interactions remain relevant considerations, particularly when supplementation is used outside documented or suspected deficiency states [@wang_zinc_2018; @biesalski_multivitaminmineral_2017].

This review has several strengths. It used a comprehensive search strategy, duplicate screening and data extraction, explicit risk-of-bias assessment, and a primary analytic approach restricted to low-risk-of-bias trials. It also evaluated a prespecified range of vitamins and minerals while excluding broader nutraceutical, herbal, and dietary interventions, allowing a more focused assessment of micronutrient supplementation as a clinically interpretable category. Several limitations should also be emphasized. Included trials varied substantially in participant selection, intervention characteristics, and outcome measures, contributing to heterogeneity. Baseline biomarker assessment was inconsistently reported, limiting mechanistic interpretation and constraining subgroup analyses. Evidence for several nutrients remained sparse and vulnerable to small-study effects. Multi-nutrient formulations were difficult to interpret because of heterogeneity in composition and dosing. Confidence was low or very low for many comparisons. As with any evidence synthesis, our conclusions are constrained by the quality and completeness of the underlying literature.

Future trials should address these limitations directly. Studies should preferentially stratify or enrich enrollment based on baseline nutrient status, measure biochemical correction alongside psychiatric outcomes, and evaluate micronutrients within clearly defined treatment contexts, including adjunctive use where appropriate. Greater consistency in outcome reporting, better characterization of dose and duration, and more systematic safety assessment will be necessary to move this literature from biologic plausibility to clinically actionable evidence [@young_systematic_2019; @tobin_targeting_2024; @biesalski_multivitaminmineral_2017].

In conclusion, vitamin D had the most consistent evidence of benefit for depressive symptoms among the micronutrients evaluated, whereas evidence for anxiety outcomes remained inconclusive and evidence for other micronutrients was limited or uncertain. These findings are more consistent with a targeted, deficiency-informed framework for future research and clinical use than with universal supplementation. Further trials should focus on well-characterized populations, incorporate biomarker assessment before and after intervention, and determine whether biochemical repletion corresponds to meaningful psychiatric improvement.
